segments.text: Geese cross the sky in a V shape.
It's not just a line - the effort isn't equal for everyone.
Every wingbeat spins the air at the wingtip into a swirl.
Just behind and outside that swirl, the air lifts upward.
A bird flying right in that spot gets extra lift, so it flaps less.
So birds tuck in diagonally behind each other.
Line enough of them up, and it forms a V.
The front bird gets no help, so that spot is the toughest.
That's why they take turns leading.
Birds fly in a V to ride the updraft made by the bird ahead.
